title: Min Stack
summary: Design a stack class that can also report its smallest value. `push(val)` puts `val` on top, `pop()` removes the most recently pushed value, `top()` returns that value without removing it, and `getMin()` returns the smallest value still in the stack. Every one of the four operations must run in O(1) time.

examples.input: push(3), push(5), push(2), getMin(), pop(), getMin(), top()
examples.explanation: Popping 2 removes the minimum, so the next getMin() falls back to 3, the smallest value left.

examples.input: push(4), push(1), push(1), pop(), getMin(), pop(), getMin()
examples.explanation: 1 was pushed twice, so after one pop it is still the minimum; after the second pop, the minimum is 4 again.

constraints: pop, top and getMin are only called when the stack holds at least one value

approaches.twist: Push each value together with the smallest value at or below it, so the top always holds the current minimum.
Keep a plain stack and scan every value in it for the smallest one each time getMin is called.
approaches.note: Works, but getMin reads every value on the stack, so it takes O(n) time. The target is O(1) per operation.

approaches.twist: Push each value onto both the stack and a min-heap, and lazily discard heap entries that were already popped from the stack.
approaches.note: Works, but every heap push and pop takes O(log n) time. The target is O(1) per operation.

signals.meaning: Last in, first out. A Python list is already a stack: append pushes and pop removes the newest value, both in O(1).

signals.phrase: smallest value still in the stack
signals.meaning: The minimum only changes on a push or a pop. Let each entry remember the smallest value at or below it; after a pop, the new top already knows the minimum of what is left.
Scanning for the minimum costs O(n) per getMin. To answer at once, have the answer ready from the pushes instead of searching when asked.

constraintReading: Up to 3·10⁴ calls. If getMin scanned the stack, 1.5·10⁴ pushes followed by 1.5·10⁴ getMin calls would read about 2·10⁸ values: O(n) per call. The O(1) target for every operation rules that out, so the minimum must be ready before anyone asks; one extra number per entry keeps the space at O(n).

hints.clarify: What should getMin return once the smallest value is popped? Try it by hand: push 4, then 2, then 7, and pop twice. After the first pop, 7 is gone and the minimum is still 2. After the second pop, 2 is gone too, and the answer has to fall back to 4. So one variable holding the smallest value so far isn't enough: when that value leaves, you need the minimum from before it arrived.
hints.approach: Stack, with the running minimum stored next to every value. The minimum can only change when a value is pushed or popped, so work it out at push time: the smallest value at or below the new top is the smaller of the new value and the minimum one level down. Keep those minimums on a second stack, `mins`, that grows and shrinks with the stack of values, `vals`. Then `getMin` just reads the top of `mins`, and `pop` removes the top of both stacks, so the minimum of what's left is already waiting one level down.
hints.whyNot: Scanning the stack for the smallest value on every `getMin` works, but it reads up to n values per call: O(n). A single variable for the minimum breaks on `pop`: once the smallest value leaves, nothing tells you the next smallest without a scan. A min-heap next to the stack does find the minimum, but every push and pop on it costs O(log n), and values already popped from the stack linger in the heap until you clean them out.

slots.setup: Two lists used as stacks, both empty at the start: `vals` holds the pushed values, and `mins` holds, at each level, the smallest value at or below that level of `vals`.
slots.loop: There's no input to scan here: the calls arrive one at a time, in order, and each one does a fixed amount of work at the top of the stacks. That's what keeps every operation O(1).
slots.update: `push` appends `val` to `vals`, and appends to `mins` the smaller of `val` and the top of `mins`, or just `val` when the stacks are empty. `pop` removes the top of both stacks, so they always have the same height.
slots.record: Nothing needs working out when a value leaves: its minimum leaves with it, and the level below already holds the minimum of everything that's left.
slots.return: `top` returns the last item of `vals`, and `getMin` returns the last item of `mins`. Each is a single read, never a search.

solution.explanation: Every method reads or changes only the end of its lists, and appending to or popping from the end of a Python list is O(1), so all four operations take O(1) time. The two stacks hold one entry per value on the stack: O(n) space. `mins` is what makes `getMin` instant: each entry was the minimum of its level and everything below it when its value was pushed, and a pop leaves the levels below exactly as they were, so the top of `mins` is always the minimum of `vals`. Naming the lists at the start of each method (`vals`, `mins`) only keeps the lines short; `self.vals` works the same.

events.label: first push
events.say: The stacks are empty, so {val} is the smallest value so far

events.label: compare
events.say: Push {val}. The minimum one level down is {mins[-1]}, so this level's minimum is the smaller of the two

events.label: push
events.say: {val} goes on top of vals, and {low} on top of mins: the smallest value at or below this level

events.label: pop
events.say: Pop {vals[-1]} from vals and its minimum {mins[-1]} from mins. The level below already knows the new minimum: {mins[-2]}

events.label: top
events.say: top() reads the last item of vals: {vals[-1]}

events.label: getMin
events.say: getMin() reads the last item of mins, {mins[-1]}, without a search

related.relation: A plain list is the stack there too, but each closer pops one opener to check a match; here every level also carries the minimum of the levels below it.
The stack there keeps only the days still waiting, popping colder ones; here every value stays until it's popped, and a second stack tracks the running minimum.
